snippets.output: Ringworm, also known as tinea corporis, is a fungal infection caused by dermatophytes, a type of fungus that infects the outer layer of the skin.
snippets.pattern_notes: Enumerated properties defining ringworm: name, type, cause, agent description.

snippets.output: The most common causative agents of ringworm are Trichophyton rubrum, Trichophyton mentagrophytes, and Microsporum canis.
Ringworm is typically spread through direct contact with an infected person or animal, contact with contaminated objects or soil, and sharing personal items such as towels, clothing, or combs.
Ringworm can be transmitted through contact with an infected animal, such as a cat or dog.
snippets.pattern_notes: Parallel examples of infected animals (cat, dog).

snippets.output: Risk factors for developing ringworm include skin-to-skin contact with an infected person or animal, sharing personal items, and having a weakened immune system.
People with compromised immune systems, such as those with diabetes or taking immunosuppressive medications, are more susceptible to ringworm infections.
snippets.pattern_notes: Lists categories of immunocompromised susceptible populations.

snippets.output: Symptoms of ringworm include a circular, itchy rash with a clear center, often accompanied by redness, scaling, and inflammation. The rash can appear anywhere on the body but is most commonly found on the arms, legs, and torso.
snippets.pattern_notes: Enumerates symptoms and common body locations.

snippets.output: Treatment for ringworm typically involves topical or oral antifungal medications, such as terbinafine or itraconazole. In severe cases, oral antifungal medications may be prescribed.
snippets.pattern_notes: Enumerates treatment options and example drugs.

snippets.output: It is essential to complete the full course of treatment to prevent recurrence and spread of the infection.
snippets.pattern_notes: Parallel reasons for completing full treatment course.
